title: The Aw Sound
kidRule: The 'aw' sound is spelled AU or AW. AU almost never ends a word, so at the end we write AW, and AW also likes to sit before N or L, as in dawn and scrawl.
hint: I hear the 'aw' sound, like when you see a cute puppy. Two spellings can make it. Think about where the sound sits in the word to pick the right team.
reminder: The 'aw' sound is spelled A-U or A-W. A-U usually goes at the start or in the middle, and A-W goes at the end of a word and often before N or L.

check.question: Why does JIGSAW end with AW and not AU?
check.correctAnswer: AU almost never ends a word, so the 'aw' sound at the end is spelled AW!
distractors: Because AU is only used in long words
Because W always comes after A in puzzle words

words.def: A puzzle made of many oddly shaped pieces that fit together to make a picture.
words.sent: We finished the jigsaw of a pirate ship.
words.story: The first jigsaw puzzles, made around 1760, were maps glued onto wood and cut apart along the borders to help children learn geography!
words.card: The hippo danced a *jig* when she finished her *jigsaw*!

words.def: A person who travels into space.
words.sent: The astronaut floated outside the space station.
words.story: This word comes from Greek words that mean 'star sailor'!
words.card: *Astro* the dog wants to be the first *astronaut* to bury a bone on the Moon!

words.def: To send a rocket or a boat on its way.
words.sent: We watched the rocket launch into the sky.
words.story: After launch, a rocket has to reach about 17,500 miles an hour to keep circling the Earth!
words.card: We *lau*gh every time we *launch* a marshmallow at the moon!

words.def: To write in a quick, messy way.
words.sent: I had to scrawl a note before the bus left.
words.story: Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks look like a scrawl at first, because he wrote backward from right to left. You need a mirror to read them easily!
words.card: My pen began to *crawl* across the page in a wobbly *scrawl*!

words.def: A sweet, red, heart-shaped fruit with tiny seeds on the outside.
words.sent: I put a strawberry on top of my pancakes.
words.story: A strawberry wears its seeds on the outside, about 200 of them on each fruit!
words.card: I drank my *strawberry* shake through a silly *straw* shaped like a slide!

words.def: A small, shallow plate that sits under a cup.
words.sent: She set her teacup down on its saucer.
words.story: People started saying 'flying saucer' in 1947, after a pilot said some strange objects moved like a saucer skipping across water!
words.card: The alien spilled tomato *sauce* all over his flying *saucer*!

words.sent: The rotten egg had an awful smell.
words.story: Long ago, awful meant 'full of awe', which is the feeling of amazement you get from something huge and wonderful!
words.card: One spoon*ful* of *awful* pickle ice cream made my ears wiggle!

words.def: Clothes that need washing or have just been washed.
words.sent: I helped fold the clean laundry.
words.story: Astronauts on the space station cannot do laundry, so they wear their clothes for a while and then throw them away!
words.card: My socks never *dry* because the *laundry* basket is a swimming pool!

words.def: Clapping to show that you liked something.
words.sent: The singer bowed as the applause filled the hall.
words.story: In sign language, people show applause by waving both hands in the air instead of clapping!
words.card: The seals gave *us* loud *applause* with their flippers!

words.def: A reptile that lived millions of years ago, and some kinds were enormous.
words.sent: The museum has the bones of a huge dinosaur.
words.story: This word was made up in 1842 from Greek words that mean 'terrible lizard'!
words.card: Oh *no*, a *dinosaur* is wearing my pajamas!
